archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A strong-armed, mobile starter whose best plays come when he leaves a collapsing pocket, paired with a passing game that works underneath and breaks down when he holds the ball or throws deep.

report.headline: Legs keep him afloat; sacks and missed deep shots keep Miami sinking.
report.take:
Willis has started all eight games for a 1-7 Dolphins team, and he is what his tools suggest: a runner first and a passer whose results swing with how long he holds the ball. He ranks 3rd among qualifying QBs in rushing yards, and his 24 scrambles are the most efficient thing Miami does, at 0.788 EPA each with 12 first downs. As a passer he sits 38th of 49 in EPA per dropback at -0.108, with a completion rate 5 points under the league average and a CPOE that ranks 41st.

The passing line hides a split. Throws from 0 to 19 air yards are good: 0.201 EPA on short throws and 0.312 on intermediate ones, with 4 of his 6 TDs underneath. Two areas sink the totals. Deep balls connect at 22.2% with 3 interceptions, and the screen and swing game behind the line has lost a combined -12.4 EPA despite a 75.7% completion rate. Then there are the sacks. His 10.3% sack rate ranks 41st, and he takes three a game. That is not a new flaw. His pressure-to-sack rate was 0.435, 0.667 and 0.6 in his three earlier stints, so holding the ball is part of who he is. The trade is real, though. His full dropback EPA, with scrambles included, totals -9.7, against -25.2 for pure passing. The escapes buy back much of what the sacks cost.

Context makes it harder. Miami's defense ranks last in EPA, and the offense passes 9.7 points less than situation predicts, 31st in the league. He has spent a lot of snaps trailing while the team tries to stay on schedule on the ground. His receivers split cleanly: Dulcich and Caleb Douglas have been efficient targets, while Kevin Coleman Jr. (-0.348 per target) and Chris Bell have drained value. The glowing 2024-25 Packers lines came on two- and three-game samples and shouldn't anchor expectations.

The recent stretch is better but not steadier. Over Weeks 7-9 his EPA per dropback rose to +0.042 and his TD rate to 5.1%, led by a sharp win over the Jets. Then he managed 128 yards against Detroit, a defense that ranks 30th. He also ran less in those three games, 13.7 yards a game below his season mark. Whether the groin is behind that is the key question for what comes next.

strengths.title: Scrambles that rescue broken plays
strengths.body: When the pocket breaks down he turns it into yardage and first downs, and these are the highest-value plays in Miami's offense. This is a stable trait: he has posted meaningful rushing totals in every season he has played. Ball security on the run, rather than the scrambling itself, is the thing to watch.

strengths.title: Efficient in the 0-19 yard window
strengths.body: On short and intermediate throws he keeps the offense on schedule and produces positive EPA. Intermediate throws have even beaten expectation on completions. This is the version of the passing game that works, and the recent upswing came from leaning on it (aDOTs of 5.1 and 7.4 in Weeks 7-8).

strengths.title: Finds his efficient targets
strengths.body: Dulcich and Douglas have been productive per target, so when the ball goes to the tight end and the second outside receiver, the offense moves. Moving volume away from Coleman would raise his floor.

concerns.title: Sacks are a career-long trait
concerns.body: A 10.3% sack rate and a 35% pressure-to-sack rate come from extending plays, with a 3.06-second time to throw. The scrambles pay back part of the cost, but not all of it. His past seasons show the same pattern, so expect it to persist rather than regress; it is on pace for 51 sacks.

concerns.title: Deep ball is a turnover source
concerns.body: He completes 22.2% of his throws of 20+ air yards, 15.8 points below expectation, with 3 of his 6 interceptions. Part of this is aggressiveness built into his game, but on 36 attempts it has cost points rather than produced shot-play upside.

concerns.title: Fumbles and dead screens
concerns.body: He has lost 3 fumbles, which ranks 45th of 49, and has 5 turnover-worthy fumbles overall. That is a carry-over cost of how long he holds the ball. The screen game behind the line has also been a steady drain, which points to blocking and receivers as much as to him. Fumble losses tend to swing with luck, but the exposure will remain.

trend.note: Weeks 7-8 were his two best passing games and lifted his last-three EPA per dropback well above his season mark. A 128-yard dud against a bottom-three defense in Week 9 showed the floor is still low, and his rushing has dipped in the same span.

nextGame.headline: Banged-up Colts back seven invites short throws and scrambles
nextGame.body:
Indianapolis is a middling pass defense, 21st in EPA allowed, and 31st in explosive pass rate allowed. It rushes the passer at only a league-average rate, 16th in sack rate, which matters for a QB whose problems start with sacks. Its opponents run more than usual (28th in pass-rate funnel), and it is the league's worst run defense by EPA. Miami's already run-leaning plan should hold, so the volume of attempts may be modest. The Colts' own passing offense ranks 31st, and the Book sees a tight, low-scoring game (IND -2.5, total 40.5). That should keep Willis out of long catch-up scripts.

Availability favors him on paper. Indy is without LB Akeem Davis-Gaither (92% of snaps), S A.J. Haulcy (83%) and CB Justin Walley (72%), with LB Jaylon Carlies questionable. That thins the middle of the field and the spy options against a scrambler. On his side, Willis is listed questionable with a groin injury. He was a full practice participant and remains QB1, but a groin is exactly the injury that could blunt his scrambling, and his rushing has already slipped. TE Will Kacmarek is questionable, which could put even more of the tight-end work on Dulcich.

keyMatchups.title: Dulcich against a soft TE defense
keyMatchups.body: Indianapolis ranks 27th in EPA allowed to opposing lead tight ends, and Dulcich has been one of Willis's most efficient targets. With a linebacker and a safety out, the seam and intermediate middle should be there. That is also the window where Willis is at his best.

keyMatchups.title: Run-heavy script against a leaky run defense
keyMatchups.body: Miami is one of the most run-leaning offenses in neutral situations. Indianapolis is last in run-defense EPA and draws extra run calls. Expect a ground-first plan that caps his attempts but sets up play-action and manageable third downs.

keyMatchups.title: Sack control against an average rush
keyMatchups.body: Indy's pass rush is league-average, not a strength. If Willis keeps his time to throw closer to his Week 7-8 levels (2.91 and 2.70 seconds), the sack drain shrinks. If he holds it like he did in Weeks 4-5, he can still give it away.

nextGame.watch: How freely he scrambles on a sore groin: if the escapes are there, his floor holds; if he stays in the pocket, the sack and deep-ball issues get exposed.

restOfSeason.body:
The skills that held up across seasons are the scrambling, the underneath efficiency and, unfortunately, the sack-taking. Expect roughly 160-210 passing yards a game on modest volume in a run-first offense, about one touchdown pass a game, and around three sacks. A team defense that ranks last will keep forcing trailing scripts. His touchdown rate over the last three games is ahead of his season norm and should settle back toward it. His deep-ball completion rate has room to improve slightly, but probably not into an asset. His fantasy floor depends on rushing: 18-35 yards a game if the groin cooperates, which is what separates a usable QB2 week from a 3-point dud like Week 9.

The upside path is the Weeks 7-8 version: a quicker release, a lower aDOT, targets aimed at Dulcich and Douglas, and scrambles as a bonus. The downside is a team at 1-7 that may eventually look elsewhere at quarterback. The dossier gives no sign of that yet, but sustained passing EPA well below average is how that conversation starts.
swingFactors: Time to throw and sack rate
Hold on the starting job on a 1-7 team

confidence.note: Eight starts give a real read on him, but his career samples are tiny, his results swing week to week, and a groin injury clouds his running.
